meta.title: What a new client costs in paid search | Elevate Marketing
meta.description: Nine documented months for an IT consultancy: four quote requests a month at £320 became twenty five at £39. What that arithmetic looks like in your business.
meta.ogTitle: What a new client costs in paid search
meta.ogDescription: A documented case file. Four quote requests a month at £320 became twenty five at £39. Work out what that means for your own contract value.

endings._comment: Typeform ending refs. Anything not listed as fit routes to /thanks, which is the safe default: showing a calendar to an unqualified lead is the exact failure this funnel exists to prevent.

hero.h1Before: A new client cost this consultancy
hero.h1Keyword: about two and a half percent of the contract
hero.lede: Nine reported months of paid search for an IT consultancy. The account went from four quote requests a month to twenty five, and the cost of each one fell by 88 percent. Below is every figure, where it came from, what it does not prove, and a calculator so you can put your own contract value against it. Most UK consultancies sell larger contracts than this one did, which makes the percentage smaller, not larger.

hero.ctaQuiet: See the month by month evidence

calculator.title: What that arithmetic looks like in your business
calculator.sub: The consultancy above sold implementations averaging £3,700, which is small for an IT consultancy. The larger your contract, the smaller the media cost looks against it. Put your own numbers in.

calculator.note: This is arithmetic, not a forecast. It applies one documented cost per quote request to numbers you supply. Yours will differ: click prices vary by market and by how competitive your keywords are, the account above ran in Norway, and no account produces its steady-state cost in month one. Treat the output as a way to sense check whether paid search is worth a conversation, not as a projection of your results.

sections.title: The month that reads like a failure
sections.sub: July 2025 is the smallest number in the whole account, and it is the one worth copying.
body: Impressions fell from a normal 80,000 to 8,130. It was deliberate. We ran a narrow campaign on a single proposition, security as a service, aimed at one buyer problem rather than the full service list.

439 clicks produced 18 quote requests. A conversion rate of 4 percent, against an account average of 0.5 percent. Roughly eight times better. Cost per request rose to £62 and volume collapsed, and we accepted both on purpose.

That trade is the argument we make in every sales conversation, and July is the month where we made it with someone else's budget rather than in a slide. A specific offer to a specific buyer converts several times better than a broad one. If you take one thing from this page and never speak to us, take that.

caution.strip: What we got wrong in the same month
body: The July report states plainly that retargeting produced no conversions. Lookalike audiences built from converters did. Retargeting was the wrong tool for a narrow, high intent offer, and we found that out on the client's money.
It is in here because an account where everything worked is an account you are not being told about in full.

sections.title: What was actually done
sections.sub: No reinvention. A sequence, in order, where each stage exists because of what the one before it produced.
steps: Measurement first. Conversion tracking and the landing pages were rebuilt so that a quote request meant a quote request, and nothing softer counted as one. Everything below is worthless without this step.
Performance Max, deliberately and temporarily. Run early to harvest search term data at volume. A means to an end, not a permanent strategy.
Search campaigns built from evidence. The harvested terms became tightly themed campaigns aimed at the queries that had actually produced quote requests, not the ones we assumed would.
Retargeting. Added to stay present with visitors who had not yet asked for a quote. How that ended is in section 02.
Lookalike audiences from converters, not visitors. The difference between those two source audiences is most of the value.

The company also had salespeople, referral flow, client expansion and resale revenue. Drawing a line from the advertising to the revenue would be exactly the claim this page exists to avoid.

limits.title: What this does not prove
limits.sub: Four things, gathered in one place rather than buried next to the numbers they qualify.

supplied.strip: Client supplied figures · not evidenced by us
supplied.intro: Everything else on this page comes from the nine monthly reports, the filed accounts or a public announcement. These three statements came from the client verbally. They do not appear in the reports, we hold no written confirmation, and we cannot evidence them.
items: Close to half of the quote requests converted into work.
Over the period the company deliberately narrowed its offer, growing one service line while others declined.
supplied.close: They are published because they are the numbers a buyer actually decides on, and because they are consistent with the documented record. Consistent is not the same as proven. The headline on this page rests on the first two, so treat that headline accordingly.

cards.title: It does not transfer cleanly to the UK
cards.body: This account ran in Norway. Click prices, competition and buyer behaviour differ, and the client's own sector focus was narrow. The mechanism transfers. The specific cost per request should not be assumed.

cards.title: It is one account, not a pattern
cards.body: Nine months, one client, one market, one service line. It shows what happened once, in documented detail. It is evidence, not a law, and anyone presenting a single account as a guarantee is selling you something.

cards.title: We did not cause the acquisition
cards.body: Avoki acquired the client one month into the engagement. Deals like that are negotiated for months before announcement, so the dates make any such claim impossible. What is a credential is that the new owner reviewed the contract and kept it running.

cards.title: The 214 are not all one service
cards.body: July's 18 requests came from a security campaign, not the main proposition. The accurate description is 214 quote requests for the client's services, with one service line as the primary proposition across most of the period.

call.title: Thirty minutes about your numbers
body: If you run an IT consultancy of 10 to 50 people and your pipeline still runs on referrals, this page was written for you. The next step is not a proposal and not a pitch. It is half an hour on what a client is worth to you, what you have already tried, and what paid acquisition would have to cost before it made sense.

Sometimes the honest answer is that it is not worth your money yet, and we say so. We work on a low monthly fee plus a fee for each client you sign, with a ceiling agreed before we start. Your total cost is known in advance and it does not move, however well the account performs. The first ninety days run as a fixed-price pilot, refunded in full if we miss the number of qualified meetings we agreed. We take on a small number of IT consultancies at a time.

Half an hour, about your numbers rather than our pitch. If it turns out paid acquisition is not right for you yet, we will say so on the call.

thanks.title: Thanks for your time | Elevate Marketing
thanks.heading: Not right now, and we would rather say so
body: Thanks for answering honestly. Sometimes the honest answer is that it is not worth your money yet, and we say so rather than book a call that wastes an hour of your day.
From what you have told us, paid acquisition would struggle to pay for itself at your current contract value and volume. That is a statement about the arithmetic, not about your business.

What would change the answer: a higher average contract value, a clearer single proposition to lead with, or a tracked way of knowing which enquiries turn into work. If any of those shift, the numbers on the case study are the ones to run again.
thanks.close: No follow up, no email sequence, and no salesperson will call. The case study stays where it is if you want to come back to it.
